**Step 1 — oxidation state of the metal.** Each chloride is \(-1\) and the complex ion is \(-1\) :

\(x + 4(-1) = -1\), so \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{V^{3\oplus}}\).

**Step 2 — box diagram of the free metal ion.** Vanadium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^3 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{V^{3\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^2}\). Writing each orbital as a box, with \(\uparrow\) for a single electron :

**\(\mathrm{V^{3\oplus}}\) (free ion)**

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\ )(\ )(\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\ )(\ )(\ )\)

**Step 3 — orbitals required.** There are four chloride ligands, each donating one electron pair, so four vacant metal orbitals are needed.

**Step 4 — hybridisation.** Chloride is a weak field ligand, so the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are not disturbed. The four vacant orbitals are taken from the outer shell — one \(\mathrm{4s}\) and three \(\mathrm{4p}\) — which hybridise to give four equivalent **\(\mathrm{sp^3}\)** orbitals directed to the corners of a tetrahedron.

**Step 5 — configuration after complex formation.**

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\ )(\ )(\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

the four pairs in \(\mathrm{4s}\) and \(\mathrm{4p}\) being the pairs donated by the four \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) ligands, which overlap with the \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybrid orbitals to form four \(\mathrm{V-Cl}\) coordinate bonds.

**Hybrid orbitals used :** \(\mathrm{sp^3}\), giving a tetrahedral complex.

**Number of unpaired electrons :** **2**, both in the \(\mathrm{3d}\) set, so the complex is paramagnetic.

**Energy-level diagram for the octahedral environment.** In a free gaseous metal ion the five d orbitals are degenerate. When six ligands approach along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes the degeneracy is destroyed and the set splits into two :

upper set \(\mathrm{e_g}\) — \((\mathrm{d_{x^2-y^2}},\ \mathrm{d_{z^2}})\), repelled UPWARD by \(0.6\,\Delta_\mathrm{o}\)

lower set \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) — \((\mathrm{d_{xy}},\ \mathrm{d_{yz}},\ \mathrm{d_{zx}})\), stabilised DOWNWARD by \(0.4\,\Delta_\mathrm{o}\)

The separation between the two levels is the crystal field splitting parameter \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) (also written 10 Dq). The \(\mathrm{e_g}\) orbitals rise more because their lobes point directly AT the incoming ligands.

**Applying it to \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\).**

Oxidation state : \(x + 6(-1) = -4\), so \(x = +2\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\). Iron is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^6 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\) is a \(\mathrm{d^6}\) ion.

\(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\) stands at the top of the spectrochemical series given in the chapter, so it is a STRONG field ligand and \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) is large — larger than the electron pairing energy. Pairing is therefore favoured and this is a LOW-SPIN complex : all six electrons go into the three \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) orbitals.

\(\mathrm{e_g} :\) \((\ )(\ )\)

\(\mathrm{t_{2g}} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

**Number of unpaired electrons : 0.**

**Magnetic behaviour :** with every electron paired the complex is **diamagnetic**.

**Colour :** the \(\mathrm{e_g}\) set is empty, so a d-d transition from the filled \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) level to the vacant \(\mathrm{e_g}\) level is still possible and the complex CAN absorb radiation and appear coloured. Note, however, that the colour is faint : because \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\) is a strong field ligand, \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) is large, so the absorption lies at the short-wavelength end and the complementary colour observed is a pale one. The chapter does not state the colour of this particular complex.

[Textbook misprint: part (c) is printed as [Cr(en2)Br2]+ with the subscript 2 INSIDE the parenthesis, verified on the source page at high magnification. A ligand written "en2" does not exist; the intended complex is [Cr(en)2Br2]+, with two ethylenediamine ligands, which is the M(AA)2B2 type the chapter works through as [Co(en)2Cl2]+. The stem is preserved as printed and the solution answers the intended reading.]

**a. \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2ClNO_2]}\)**

The complex is neutral, so \(x + 2(0) + (-1) + (-1) = 0\) gives \(\mathrm{Pt^{2\oplus}}\) with four ligands — a square planar complex of the \(\mathrm{MA_2BC}\) type, which the chapter says exists as cis and trans isomers.

Draw platinum at the centre of a square with the four ligands at its corners :

*cis isomer* — the two \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands on ADJACENT corners, with \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) occupying the other two adjacent corners.

*trans isomer* — the two \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands on OPPOSITE corners, so that \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) are also opposite each other.

A further pair of isomers is possible here, because \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\) is an ambidentate ligand : bound through nitrogen it is the nitro complex \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl(NO_2)]}\), and bound through oxygen it is the nitrito complex \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl(ONO)]}\). These two are **linkage isomers**.

**b. \(\mathrm{[Ru(NH_3)_4Cl_2]}\)**

Six ligands, so an octahedral complex of the \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\) type — the same type as the chapter's worked \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\).

*cis isomer* — the two chloride ligands on ADJACENT corners of the octahedron (at \(90^\circ\) to each other), the four ammine ligands filling the remaining positions.

*trans isomer* — the two chloride ligands OPPOSITE each other (at \(180^\circ\)), with the four ammine ligands in the square plane between them.

**c. \(\mathrm{[Cr(en_2)Br_2]^{\oplus}}\)**

Read as \(\mathrm{[Cr(en)_2Br_2]^{\oplus}}\), this is an octahedral complex of the \(\mathrm{M(AA)_2B_2}\) type, the same type as the chapter's \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\).

*cis isomer* — the two bromide ligands ADJACENT, with the two en rings spanning the remaining four positions. This isomer has no plane of symmetry, so it is itself chiral and exists as a d, l pair of enantiomers.

*trans isomer* — the two bromide ligands OPPOSITE each other, the two en rings lying in the square plane between them. This one has a plane of symmetry and is not chiral.

**a. \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_3]^{4\oplus}}\)**

Ethylenediamine is neutral and bidentate, so platinum is \(+4\) and the coordination number is \(3 \times 2 = 6\) — an octahedral tris-chelate of the \(\mathrm{M(AA)_3}\) type, the same type as the chapter's \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3\oplus}}\).

*Geometric isomers :* **none.** All six positions are occupied by donor atoms of the same kind of ligand, so there is no pair of identical ligands that can be moved from an adjacent to an opposite position — cis and trans do not arise.

*Enantiomers :* **yes, a d, l pair.** Draw platinum at the centre of an octahedron with the three en rings each spanning one edge. The three rings form a propeller. Its mirror image is a propeller of the opposite twist, and no rotation brings the two into coincidence, so they are non-superimposable mirror images — the dextro (d) and laevo (l) forms.

**b. \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2ClBr]^{2\oplus}}\)**

Here \(x + 2(0) + (-1) + (-1) = +2\) gives platinum \(+4\), with a coordination number of \(2 \times 2 + 1 + 1 = 6\) — an octahedral complex of the \(\mathrm{M(AA)_2BC}\) type.

*Geometric isomers :* **two.**

*cis isomer* — \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) on ADJACENT positions, the two en rings spanning the remaining four.

*trans isomer* — \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) OPPOSITE each other, the two en rings lying in the square plane between them.

*Enantiomers :* only the **cis** isomer is chiral. Its mirror image, with the two en rings twisted the opposite way, cannot be superimposed on it, so the cis form exists as a d, l pair. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry containing the two en rings and is achiral — this is exactly the result the chapter states for \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2\oplus}}\), where only the cis isomer exists as a pair of enantiomers.

**Ligands** are the ions or molecules that surround the central metal atom or ion in a coordination compound. They are linked to the metal through coordinate bonds, and it is the ligand that contributes the shared electron pair — so a ligand is an electron pair donor, that is, a Lewis base.

The chapter classifies them as follows.

**1. Monodentate ligands** — a single donor atom shares an electron pair with the metal ion. **Example :** \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) (also \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)).

**2. Polydentate ligands** — two or more donor atoms of the same ligand are linked to the central metal ion.

  A ligand with two donor atoms is **bidentate**. **Example :** ethylenediamine, which binds through the lone pair on each of its two nitrogen atoms (also the oxalate ion \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2\ominus}}\), which binds through two oxygen atoms).

  A ligand with six donor atoms is **hexadentate**. **Example :** the ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion, \(\mathrm{(EDTA)^{4\ominus}}\), which binds through four oxygen and two nitrogen atoms.

**3. Ambidentate ligands** — the ligand has two DIFFERENT donor atoms and uses the electron pair of either one to form the coordinate bond. **Example :** the nitrite ion \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\), which can link through nitrogen or through oxygen (also \(\mathrm{SCN^{\ominus}}\), which can link through sulphur or nitrogen).

This is the chapter's classification on the basis of the charge on the coordination sphere.

**Cationic complexes** — a positively charged coordination sphere, or a coordination compound having a positively charged coordination sphere. **Example :** \(\mathrm{[Zn(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\). Another is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\), whose sphere \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]^{2\oplus}}\) is made electrically neutral by the \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) counter ion.

**Anionic complexes** — a negatively charged coordination sphere, or a compound having one. **Example :** \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\). Another is \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\), in which the sphere \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\) is balanced by three \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) ions.

**Neutral complexes** — the complex possesses neither a cationic nor an anionic sphere; it carries no charge at all and so has no counter ion. **Example :** \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) (also \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\)).

Complex formation is an equilibrium between the metal ion and the ligands, and the position of that equilibrium is what 'stability' measures.

For a metal ion \(\mathrm{M^{a\oplus}}\) and \(n\) ligands \(\mathrm{L^{x\ominus}}\) :

\(\mathrm{M^{a\oplus}} + n\,\mathrm{L^{x\ominus}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[ML_n]^{a\oplus + nx\ominus}}\)

and the equilibrium constant, called the **stability constant** \(K\), is

\(K = \dfrac{[\mathrm{ML_n}]}{[\mathrm{M^{a\oplus}}][\mathrm{L^{x\ominus}}]^n}\)

\(K\) is the ratio of the concentration of the complex to those of the free metal ion and free ligands. A large \(K\) therefore means the equilibrium lies far to the right, so most of the metal is present as the complex and very little as free ion :

**the higher the value of \(K\), the greater the thermodynamic stability of the complex.**

The chapter's own data illustrate this :

\(\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}} + 2\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^{\ominus}}\), \(K = 5.5 \times 10^{18}\)

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}} + 4\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[Cu(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\), \(K = 2.0 \times 10^{27}\)

\(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}} + 6\mathrm{NH_3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\), \(K = 5.0 \times 10^{33}\)

Since \(5.0 \times 10^{33}\) is the largest of the three, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^{\ominus}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cu(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\).

The chapter names **two** factors.

**a. Charge to size ratio of the metal ion.** The higher the ratio, the greater the stability. For the divalent metal ion complexes the stability follows the Irving-William order

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}} > \mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}} > \mathrm{Co^{2\oplus}} > \mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}} > \mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}} > \mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\)

The chapter's illustration : \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\) carry the same \(+2\) charge, but the ionic radius of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) is 69 pm against 97 pm for \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\). The charge to size ratio of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) is therefore the greater, and it forms the more stable complexes.

**b. Nature of the ligand.** What matters is how easily the ligand can donate its lone pair to the central metal ion — that is, the **basicity** of the ligand. Ligands that are stronger bases tend to form more stable complexes.

Both factors act through the same underlying idea stated at the start of the section : the metal-ligand interaction is a Lewis acid-Lewis base interaction, and the stronger that interaction, the greater the stability of the complex.
